headline: High risk of prompt-injection, data leakage, and cascading errors when Cursor’s local workspace/clipboard agent is paired with pipecat’s shared-bus, networked voice pipeline.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Cursor ingests workspace files, open buffers, and clipboard contents, while pipecat can move text through a shared bus and stdin/stdout. That creates a plausible instruction-smuggling path if pipecat forwards untrusted text into Cursor’s editor context. The pair is not directly documented, so uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF pipecat forwards user-controlled text into Cursor open buffers or clipboard
IF Cursor agent mode reads those buffers as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable clipboard bridging between the two agents
Route pipecat text through a sanitizer before Cursor sees it
Use separate workspaces for each agent
Mark all cross-agent text as untrusted in prompts
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to shared messages

B_data_leakage.rationale: Cursor touches source code, open files, and clipboard contents and has broad network egress to model providers and MCP servers. Pipecat handles text, audio, video, and conversation state on a shared bus. If sensitive workspace data reaches pipecat or Cursor’s context is transmitted outward, leakage can occur by default through normal operation, so the blast radius is substantial.
conditions: IF Cursor opens files containing secrets or regulated data
IF pipecat receives that content on its shared bus or forwards it to external STT/LLM/TTS services
mitigations: Keep sensitive files out of Cursor’s workspace
Disable external providers in pipecat for sensitive sessions
Use separate OS users or containers
Rotate any secrets exposed in shared buffers
requires-engineering: enforce data-loss-prevention filters on bus traffic

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Cursor can write the filesystem, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses; pipecat can run across processes and machines with shared-bus state. If both operate on the same repo or mutable resource, concurrent writes and git mutations can race and corrupt state. The profiles show overlapping mutable surfaces, so this is a default-dangerous conflict.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or git repository
IF pipecat workers and Cursor sessions run concurrently without locking
mitigations: Assign separate directories per agent
Pause one agent before the other writes
Use git locks or serialized commits
Restrict Cursor to read-only mode during pipecat runs
requires-engineering: add cross-process file locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: Cursor can generate code or operational text, and pipecat can consume text in a shared-bus pipeline and then call external services. That makes it plausible for Cursor output to become authoritative input for downstream actions without verification. The pair is not directly evidenced, so medium is appropriate rather than high.
conditions: IF pipecat treats Cursor-generated text as authoritative
IF downstream services act on that text without a verification step
mitigations: Insert a human review step before actions
Require schema validation on Cursor outputs
Log and diff all downstream transformations
Limit pipecat to read-only summarization
requires-engineering: add confidence gates before tool calls

E_compliance.rationale: Cursor explicitly handles source code, open files, and clipboard contents, while pipecat handles conversation state plus analytics/metrics and can send data to multiple third-party providers. If regulated or residency-bound data enters both systems, retention and transfer policies can diverge. The profiles do not specify matching compliance controls, so the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF regulated data is present in Cursor open files or clipboard
IF pipecat routes that data to external providers or retains analytics beyond policy
mitigations: Exclude regulated data from shared sessions
Disable analytics for sensitive runs
Use region-locked providers only
Document retention settings for both tools
requires-engineering: align residency and retention policies
